report.headline: Usage projected to climb from 18.4% to 23.0% in the move to the EuroLeague, but the shooting-efficiency projection is not trustworthy for this transition.

projection.text: The model projects a usage rate of 23.0% in the EuroLeague, up from 18.4% in the 2010-11 NBA season, moving the subject from below the NBA average (-0.33 sd) to above the EuroLeague average of 20.3%.

risks.text: The true shooting projection of 57.2% cannot be trusted: the model's error on this metric (4.7%) is no better than the trivial baseline (4.7%), so it should be treated as carrying no signal.

Even where the model is informative, the 80% usage interval (18.6%-27.5%) covers about a third of the plausible EuroLeague usage range, so any single-season figure is highly uncertain despite the group-level signal being real.
The estimate is built on only 115 historical NBA->EL transitions, a comparatively thin sample next to the G League-anchored cohorts the model can otherwise draw on.

The fitted usage slope of 0.986 implies near-full carryover of standing, but combined with the -0.33 sd source usage, it also means the projected rise is driven mostly by league context (lower EuroLeague average is not the case here) rather than a clear talent signal.

strengths.text: Source-season true shooting of 56.7% was 0.51 sd above the NBA average that season, indicating efficient scoring relative to NBA peers.
Projected usage of 23.0% sits above the EuroLeague's minutes-weighted average of 20.3%, pointing to an expanded offensive role compared to the NBA season.
The usage projection model beats the trivial league-mean baseline (3.3% mean absolute error vs. 4.3%), so this particular projection carries real information rather than noise.
Played a full, durable season in the source year: 1,999 minutes across 64 games.

uncertainty.text: The 80% interval for usage runs from 18.6% to 27.5%, a span of roughly two standard deviations of EuroLeague usage (sd 4.4%), so the model can say this is a group likely to see a larger role but cannot pin down where in that range the subject lands; the 95% interval widens further to 16.2%-29.8%. Separately, the cohort of NBA->EL movers this estimate rests on sat 0.31 sd below their own league's average, so the usual assumption of a strongly above-average mover does not clearly apply here.
